newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The rand continued to retreat on Tuesday in the face of an advancing dollar and added another cent to Monday's one cent loss against the U.S. unit.
At 1400 GMT, the local unit was pegged at 4.4320/4350 against the dollar, slightly off a day's weakest level of 4.4350 -- a two-week low -- from 4.4235/4265 on Monday.

The dollar strode to a fresh four-year high of 126.52 yen and moved to a five-week high of 1.7183 marks earlier in the day, which local traders said triggered both importer and offshore demand for the U.S. currency.
"We've seen a lot of demand out of London for dollars and the local importers are still buying," a trader said.
That demand carried the rand to the 4.4350 level where dealers said heavy exporter selling forced it to retrace some of its losses.
"We saw exporters at 4.4360...mining houses looking to sell dollars," a dealer said.
Despite the retracement, dealers felt the rand looked set to stage an assault on the 4.45 level within the next few days.

"I think it is a matter of time before we see a weaker rand given the dollar strength," a dealer said. "If the dollar continues stronger, or even maintains these gains, we could see 4.45 within a couple of days."
Another trader echoed his sentiments: "We have been caught in a range from a fundamental point of view...with the strong dollar we will be looking for 4.45 by the end of the week," he said.
The dollar's resurgence against the mark and yen resulted in gains for the rand on both currencies.

The local currency touched a fresh 14-month high against the yen and mark earlier in the day when it touched 28.5346 and 0.3881 marks. Against sterling, the rand was little changed at 7.1980/2073 as cable held its ground.
The bond market put in a repeat of Monday's performance, drifting sideways in quiet and directionless trade.
The key R150 was last pegged at a 15.135 percent yield from 15.155 percent on Monday.
Traders said the recent apathy in the market appeared to be linked to the better returns on offer in the short-end.
"I think investors believe that with short-term rates as high as they are and no sign of them coming down, they are better off investing there than in the long-end," a trader said.
Three-month deposit rates held steady at 16.65 percent on the day, while the 90-day BA rate held its recent 15.95 to 16.15 percent range.
Dealers have pinned the high level of short-term rates on the persistently high shortage, which the Reserve Bank pegged at at 9.972 billion rand on Monday from 10.674 billion rand on Saturday.
Another bond trader said institutional investors were also holding to the sidelines for further clues on the U.S. Treasury bond market's short-term direction.
"The institutions are a bit worried about U.S. bonds. They want to see whether that market is in a sustainable bear run or is busy topping out," he said.

The yield on the 30-year T-bond rose to a seven-month high of 7.12 percent last week amid fears that the Federal Reserve will repeat its March 25 rate hike with a further 25-basis point tightening at its next meeting on May 20.
The T-bond stood at 7.10 percent in early Tuesday New York trade.
Traders felt that while the longer-term outlook for the local bond market was bullish, buying would only return once short-term rates started coming down.
Given that expectations of an interest rate cut are now turning towards the end of this year, dealers said the anticipated bull run might only get going beyond July.
Foreigners were net buyers of 99.99 million rand's worth of South African bonds on Monday after buying 471.57 million rand's worth on Friday, the Bond Exchange said.
Nominal cumulative volumes were pegged at a paltry 2.73 billion rand on Monday from 5.59 billion rand on Friday.
-- Paul Richardson, Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
